messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

# Managed database or your own?

## What you're actually buying

A managed service sells you an on-call rotation. Failover, minor-version patches, point-in-time restore, the 3 a.m. disk-full alert — that work moves to a vendor who runs ten thousand of these. The engine is the same Postgres or MySQL you'd install yourself. What changes is who gets paged.

## The cost gap is real, and usually misread

Managed instances run roughly 2–4x the price of equivalent raw compute, and IOPS and egress billing widen the spread further. Teams compare that against a hardware quote and conclude self-hosting wins. It doesn't, unless you price the engineer. One DBA who can actually debug a stuck vacuum costs more per year than most teams' entire managed bill.

## Run your own when

- You need something the provider blocks: an unsupported extension, a kernel knob, custom WAL shipping, a storage layout outside the menu.
- Residency or contractual terms keep the data out of someone else's tenancy.
- The multiplier has grown into seven figures and you already employ people who do this full time.
- You need the database in the same rack as your compute, in a facility no provider sells into.

## Otherwise, take the managed option

The failure mode of self-hosting isn't steady state — steady state is quiet for months. It's the first unplanned restore, run by whoever is awake, against a backup nobody has tested.

Both directions stay open. A pg_dump and a maintenance window move you either way, and that reversibility is worth more than getting the choice right on day one.

---

~255 words. Checked against the repo's `slopwatch` ruleset — passes clean. The cost multiplier (2–4x) is a rough industry range, not a figure I measured; swap in your own numbers if this is going in front of a buyer.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.
